findings.where: First screen at phone width: Mark's portrait and its 'Placeholder' caption
findings.fault: On the phone, the portrait sits centred in the column with a gap on both sides, and its caption is centred too. Everything around it lines up on the frame's left inner edge: the logo, the name, the nav, Mark's line, the sentence and the address strip. Every other caption on the sheet also starts at the left: the article photograph's caption, and the desktop caption, which is aligned to the portrait's edge. On the phone, the one image in the first screen is the only part that does not share the left edge. The tile's own texture note says the portrait is 'set flush' against the frame, which the desktop version does and the phone version doesn't.
findings.who_objects: The founder, judging the first screen at phone width. A centred photo with a centred caption over left-aligned text looks like a template default, not a set page. That works against the 'refined, legal journal' impression this direction is meant to give.

findings.where: First screen at desktop width: the nav (Profile, Articles, Blog) beside the name lockup
findings.fault: The nav's baseline lines up with nothing in the lockup next to it. It sits below the baseline of 'Mark M. Moseley' and above the baseline of 'Formerly Lead Lawyer, PPP Group, World Bank', so it floats between the two lines. It is not aligned to the top of the lockup or to the baseline of either line.
findings.who_objects: A designer or the founder looking at the header. On a sheet whose claim is careful, document-like setting, a nav that is a few pixels off both lines next to it looks unfinished.

findings.where: Article specimen title 'The World's Best Public-Private Partnership Law', at desktop and phone width
findings.fault: The apostrophe in 'World's' renders as a straight typewriter tick. Everywhere else the article uses typographer's quotes: ‘chapter topics’, ‘Abundance’, and the curly double quotes around the client's question. At title size the straight mark stands out more than anywhere else.
findings.who_objects: Angélique and Mark, whose articles this template will set. A legal-journal setting with a typewriter apostrophe in its largest line reads as careless, and a reader who knows typography sees it first.

findings.fault: The easing curve is drawn in the logo blue. The tile's own palette gives blue three jobs only (wordmark, links, focus), and the brief keeps blue for the wordmark and links. Here blue is used on a static diagram line, the one place on the sheet where it has none of those jobs.
findings.who_objects: The founder, judging whether the direction keeps blue to its stated roles. The sheet states a rule and then breaks it in its own specimen, which weakens the case that blue means 'wordmark or link' on this site.
